extracted.intended_audience: Reuters journalists, editors, bureau chiefs, regional editors and approved stringers (newsroom staff and freelancers handling Reuters copy)
extracted.subtask_description: Editorial and legal guidance for newsroom reporting, sourcing, safety, handling complaints, stringers, hoaxes, and incident reporting in a global news organisation (Reuters). Focuses on when to escalate (ATTENTION EDITOR), verification, legal risks and staff safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: ATTENTION EDITOR protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Bureaus should send potentially risky stories to the relevant desk with the words ATTENTION EDITOR in the slug and an accompanying message explaining the risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such stories should be handled by a regional specialist editor or the senior desk editor on duty, with reference to in-house or external lawyers if required. Err on the side of caution if you have any concerns about the legality of a story, about issues of taste, balance or fairness or about the good name and reputation of Reuters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bankruptcy stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Bankruptcy stories should be slugged ATTENTION EDITOR. Be very careful when using adjectives to describe a company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A company becomes formally bankrupt or insolvent when a court rules it is unable to meet its debts; terms (bankruptcy, insolvency, liquidation) have different legal meanings in different countries — be precise and offer clear definitions when necessary. Any story about a potential bankruptcy from a third party must contain comment from the company concerned or at least indicate serious efforts to seek that comment. Be as precise as possible in reporting what a company or court says, especially with translations (examples: French faillite vs banqueroute). Applications under bankruptcy rules may be technical manoeuvres and could lead to libel actions if misinterpreted. Avoid over-colourful reporting that implies hopelessness if a company later recovers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil lawsuits reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid reporting threats to file a lawsuit unless parties are sufficiently high-profile and the case is market-moving; if covered, file ATTENTION EDITOR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When covering threatened or real lawsuits, include comment from both parties. If comment is not immediately available and there's overriding news reason to run the story, make clear what efforts were made to reach the party (e.g., 'A spokesman for Company X did not respond to two voicemail messages seeking comment.'). Consider possible motives of sources to avoid being used to exert pressure for out-of-court settlements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contentious claims, allegations and vituperative attacks (unnamed sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not allow sources to make allegations, contentious statements or vituperative attacks behind a cloak of anonymity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If quoting unnamed sources about what is happening to the other side, use them only for facts, not opinions. If a source wants to make a vituperative attack, they must speak on the record. Exception: a senior official making a considered policy statement which is obviously newsworthy may be allowed unnamed if story makes clear informant volunteered the information and is an official. Any story accusing a person or entity of wrongdoing, shame or illicit activities should be filed ATTENTION EDITOR and must normally carry comment from the other party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphic details, obscenities and blasphemy
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not publish graphic details and obscene or blasphemous language gratuitously or to titillate; there must be a valid news reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such material will usually require a decision by a senior editor and should be sent ATTENTION EDITOR with an explanation of why the material has been used. Consider whether the material is necessary to understanding; be mindful of different market thresholds. If published, bring to readers' attention in brackets at the top of the story (e.g., 'Note strong language in paragraph 6') and spell out expletives. Online desks pushing news directly to consumers must handle copy appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legally dangerous material (general principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should be familiar with the general principles of libel, defamation and privacy rights and with the specific laws where they operate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of risks (legal action, restrictions, expulsion), any story that may be legally dangerous should be filed ATTENTION EDITOR. The decision to publish such material should be taken by a senior editor, including consultation with lawyers if required. The guide is not a substitute for legal advice; consult Legal Dangers eLearning and in-house counsel as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stories about Reuters, its staff or operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Any story about Reuters, its staff or its operations should be filed ATTENTION EDITOR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These stories should normally be written by the senior journalist in the bureau and cleared for publication by the relevant regional specialist editor. Seek comment from an authorised company spokesman and make them aware in case of press enquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific, medical breakthroughs and sensational stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories about major scientific discoveries or medical breakthroughs should be handled with the utmost care and normally by a specialist correspondent; if not possible, file ATTENTION EDITOR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such stories must come from a reputable named source and should be checked with experts for verification. Be sceptical of sensational claims (e.g., cloning, cure for AIDS, life on Mars, babies with three heads); consult specialists and send ATTENTION EDITOR if in doubt. Consider investor/community expertise for medical/drug studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawals
rubrics_metrics.description: Any story that has to be withdrawn for any reason should be filed ATTENTION EDITOR with an explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withdrawals are legally and reputationally sensitive and require senior oversight and documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hoax avoidance and verification checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use news until you are certain of its authenticity; guard against hoax attempts by being suspicious and checking sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical drill: regard telephone information as suspect unless you know caller; ask for full name/title/telephone and check independently (switchboard, online searches). Telephone the person back to confirm. Use same precautions with unsolicited email/fax/IM/SMS/mail. Be on guard for April Fool hoaxes or fantastical claims and follow checking even if it delays a story. Use nothing found on the Internet that isn't verifiable; confirm via telephone or other means. Capture and save a screenshot of the web page for defence against charges. We have no greater protection if we pick up a hoax from another news organisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dealing with complaints — underlying principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Respond promptly and properly to complaints; attitude matters and common sense should be applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record and retain particulars of callers or correspondents (name, title, company/group, telephone). Treat complaints as feedback; avoid hostility. There is no one-size-fits-all process; combine guidelines with situation-specific judgment. Prompt, proper response can avoid legal problems and bad publicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: First responses to complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: If issue raised by telephone, record essence and particulars; retain information even if resolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you can deal with the complaint immediately (e.g., misspelt name), do so. If it involves another journalist, put that person on the line. If you cannot handle, advise the complainant you will discuss with other staff and get back to them; then inform a senior staffer. Mirror the medium of the complaint (phone for phone, email for email). Centres receiving many routine comments may develop form letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Further steps and escalation on complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: Escalate complaints that involve subjective judgments, disputes about facts, libel claims, requests to withdraw or repeated complainants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-check and explore references; if we are wrong, issue correction and advise complainant. Inform senior editors as appropriate (e.g., government department complaints may affect access). Advise marketing/sales when client relationships may be affected. Contact in-house legal department immediately for threats to sue and inform public relations for advice. Use editorial incident reporting for significant cases and the company's global electronic logging of serious incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial recordkeeping for complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: Retain letters, emails and notes related to complaints even if settled; bureau chiefs should retain a central file of records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A central file helps if complainant reopens matter and supports consistency across bureaus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hiring stringers
rubrics_metrics.description: Utmost care in hiring stringers; only hire reputable journalists who will adhere to Reuters standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No individual should hire a stringer without explicit approval of the bureau chief/editor in charge. Preference to professional journalists; bureaus should not hire non-journalists without regional managing editor and specialist editor approval. Never hire government officials, armed forces/police/intelligence members or PR employees as stringers. Brief stringers on standards of accuracy, objectivity, sourcing and freedom from bias; ask them to acknowledge reading an abridged Code of Conduct. Offer training for regular contributors. Tell stringers Reuters reserves right to rewrite material and to use byline but discuss circumstances where byline may be inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protecting stringer identity when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases where it could be dangerous for a stringer's identity to be revealed, the identity should not be divulged without explicit approval from a senior editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normal practice should be for stringers to identify themselves as working on behalf of Reuters, but exceptions exist for safety; decisions should be escalated as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling material from stringers (accuracy and skepticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bureaus and desks handling stringer copy must expect the same standards of accuracy, objectivity, sourcing and freedom from bias as from staff, and exercise particular caution because stringers may be less accountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the 'smell' test — challenge facts/quotes that don't smell right. Beware anonymous sources especially if unfamiliar with stringer. Insert only relevant background/context. Prefer staff coverage for diarised news of significant interest unless satisfied stringer will do as good a job. On major breaking news, ensure staff coverage rapidly unless strong grounds to continue with stringer alone. Consult manager if in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stringer byline and ghosting policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious about using stringer bylines on contentious material; never 'ghost' a news story under a stringer byline if they contributed nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never add a byline without consulting the stringer, a staff correspondent, the bureau chief or specialist editor. When significant changes are made to bylined copy, make reasonable efforts to send story back to correspondent for final check; if not reachable, senior editor decides whether to use byline. Apply same byline policy to stringer and staff copy. Never 'ghost' an analysis under a stringer's byline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dealing with threats, claims of responsibility and hostage-taking
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not encourage groups using violence to use Reuters as a publicity vehicle; do not pay for such material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise judgement whether to report statements/calls as 'received by Reuters' or 'received by an international news agency' — often consult senior editor. Do not withhold textual information from other news organisations unless agreed; treat threats like rumours and avoid circulating unvalidated threats. If threat is made to Reuters office, report immediately to police and regional general news editor. Be convinced of caller credibility and have publishable reaction from authorities before issuing a story. Authenticated statements from recognized groups can be used on news merit if incident has taken place; unauthenticated or unknown-group statements treated with grave reserve. For hostage material: advise hostage's organisation/family, get original/copy to the organisation quickly, inform police, and ensure internal cross-notification between Reuters services (text, video, photos).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangerous situations — safety and consent
rubrics_metrics.description: The safety of journalists is paramount; no story or image is worth a life and all dangerous assignments are voluntary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists may decline hazardous assignments without penalty. Avoid obvious danger and unreasonable risks. You may move into a dangerous environment only with authorisation of your superior; consult senior regional editor. Assignments limited to experienced personnel or under their direct supervision. No one assigned to danger zone unless they completed Hostile Environment training. Bureau chief and regional Managing Editor responsible for safety and may order you not to run risks you consider acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational safety in danger zones
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical safety measures for travel and operations in dangerous areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not move alone; travel as a passenger with a known trusted driver; identify vehicle as press car unless it increases risk; when possible travel in convoy. Do not travel in military-style vehicles unless with regular military unit. Carry identification including Reuters card unless it jeopardises safety. Advise base of movements and increases in danger. Do not carry weapons or travel with journalists who do. Do not accompany or operate close to people carrying weapons without explicit authorisation. Weigh differing risk profiles for correspondents vs camera operators. Learn key local language phrases and local meanings of signs/gestures. Be cautious about maps with markings. Seek agreement of troops before photographing; if unable to get agreement, get bureau chief authorisation and discuss safest approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal protective gear and health precautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Wear protective clothing such as helmet and body armour in war zones where appropriate; carry gas mask/protective clothing if biological/chemical risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider wearing civilian clothes unless accredited as war correspondent; avoid military or paramilitary clothing. Carry medically relevant identification (bracelet with caduceus and blood group/allergies). Party should have basic first-aid kit and sterile syringes. Covering human suffering can be traumatic; assistance available via Editorial Assistance Program or HR and is confidential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behaviour if threatened in the field
rubrics_metrics.description: If confronted by threatening people, try to stay relaxed and act friendly; avoid aggressive or nervous behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry cigarettes or small luxuries as icebreakers. Never cross the line between impartial observer and participant; do not give information to one side about operations on the other. If challenged, offer as much information about yourself as you can without compromising safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to file an incident report
rubrics_metrics.description: An incident report must be filed when staff are injured/killed/imperilled/harassed; Reuters is threatened with legal action; Reuters withdraws a story/graphic/video; Reuters makes a mistake that adversely affects a customer and prompts angry calls; Reuters is target of a hoax; serious allegations against employees; service is seriously disrupted; issue could embarrass the company; or involvement in controversy that could result in analyst's/reporter's questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The list is not exhaustive; err on the side of caution in informing supervisors. Incident reporting is essential to keep senior officials up to date and to spot trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to file an incident report
rubrics_metrics.description: When a serious incident occurs, contact your direct supervisor and file an incident report using the Corporate Incident Notification Site.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Update the report on the site until the matter is closed. The managing editor in each region must ensure bureau chiefs and specialist editors are aware of relevant incidents elsewhere. Managing editors are responsible for keeping a register of incidents and complaints in their regions; the database is maintained centrally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal Dangers guide — general tips contents
rubrics_metrics.description: The Legal Dangers guide includes General Tips such as Notes and other records, Accuracy, Balance, Use of quotes, Unnamed sources, A healthy dose of scepticism, Your work has a global reach, Attention editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These topics serve as core editorial/legal checkpoints to recognise legal danger and find required assistance (eLearning modules and additional material available). Journalists are encouraged to attend face-to-face legal training where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation and related topics (contents outline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guide covers Defamation: what is defamation; what is a defamatory statement; defamation and images; who may sue; elements of action (is it defamatory? does it identify claimant? has the statement been published?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also covers common defences (Truth/justification; Fair comment; Absolute privilege; Statutory qualified privilege; Common-law qualified privilege). These are legal standards journalists should recognise and consult counsel about when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contempt and court reporting restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal dangers guide includes sections on Contempt and court reporting restrictions and protecting your sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should be familiar with local contempt rules, how court restrictions affect reporting and the balance between reporting and protecting sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright and use of third-party material
rubrics_metrics.description: Guide covers Copyright infringement and Copyright and stringers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists must respect copyright rules for images and text, ensure clearance and appropriately handle stringer-supplied copyrighted material.
